summary: Indexed 46 Boot Camp lessons and 14 Boot Camp 2.0 lessons from the public playlists.
Day 1 is a contract and a journal rule. No setup. The early sweep story stays a hypothesis until the liquidity lessons.

Live money is a later test of whether the free boot camp made this student profitable. Stake, max loss, and pass/fail are fixed before the first order. Agent is flat until the lessons and 20 paper sessions exist.
Notebook is study notes of the free boot camps. The score is how many lessons are written down. Removed the experiment, how-it-works, and how-the-agent-trades pages.
Day 2 is the first chart lesson.
Day 3 is a mindset day.
Day 4 defines a trend as momentum.
Day 5 is the second mindset lesson, on a method of goal setting he says he learned in a basketball program.
Day 6 defines a break of structure as a change in the trend from Day 4.
Day 7 is a mindset day about staying a separate person from the teacher.
Day 8 is the opening of the topic he calls the center of his method: liquidity.
Day 9 is a pause, not a chart lesson.
Day 10 is where to find liquidity, after the prior lesson on what it is.
Day 11 is a psychology lesson timed as the series starts to talk about execution.
Day 12 closes the liquidity series by showing the idea on charts and saying what it is for.
Day 13 is his first pass at risk, and he defines it narrowly: how much is exposed, and how often.
Day 14 introduces fair value gaps by definition only.
Day 15 is a written exercise in finding problems and then finding what they grow from.
Day 16 is how to see a fair value gap, after the prior definition.
Patience is the reason rushed entries happen.
This is the recap day for fair value gaps.
He builds the lesson on that day's CPI release, after watching people try to trade before, during, and after the print.
This is the explanation day for order blocks.
The assigned topic is how to take a win, and he says it matters more than how to take a loss.
This is the spotting day.
He is late for a check-in he promised after two weeks.
He uses this day to close the order-block series by doing the spotting homework in public.
Day 25 is a psychology talk set just before equilibrium.
Equilibrium is the last building block in this stretch, and he calls it one of the easier ones.
Day 27 is the other side of the confidence line from the overconfidence talk.
Day 28 puts the halfway line on charts.
He calls the written plan the page that makes a later strategy hard to violate.
This is the first execution lesson, and he keeps it off the charts.
He treats this day as a return to the opening idea of the series.
Part two puts the first two execution stacks on a chart.
Part three covers the two remaining stacks on charts.
He says execution is no longer the missing piece.
He teaches daily bias again, this time before the open, with the charts on screen.
He uses the weekly to interpret a daily break.
He places take-profit levels on the same building blocks used for entries: order blocks, fair value gaps, and draws on liquidity.
The stop is an invalidation, not a fixed count of points.
He names three ways to choose a size.
This is a check-in, not a new chart method.
Day 41 is about a stretch of losses, not a new model.
Day 42 answers a request for a backtest method, and he says he will describe what he actually uses.
Day 43 is a walkthrough of one upcoming week, and he says the procedure is the same one he uses on an ordinary open.
Day 44 is about which markets to leave alone.
Day 45 says the slowdown comes from adding pieces, not from a hole in the method.
Day 46 is the journal layout he says people asked for after the previous talk.
He says this season puts the day's recap and a short lesson in the same video.
The gold trade is his usual forex sequence.
He opens by saying the recap should be about the trade itself.
The lesson is his announcement of a broker change, and the reasons he gives for the choice.
He opens with the week, because the calendar changes where he is willing to look for a bias.
This is a short second video from the same day, recorded because he took an index trade after the gold trade and the first target had just been hit.
He starts with the index trade from the prior update.
This session is a short recap of one long, used to talk about size when the chart and the calendar pull in different directions.
He recaps two trades and spends the lesson on how to choose when several charts look alive at once.
He recaps three trades and uses them to show a stop that does not kill the idea, as long as the bias is still intact and some of the day's risk is still unused.
The prior session had no recap because he never took a trade.
The session is one long, on pound/dollar, and a talk about where a target belongs.
He calls the session a red day.
He recaps one loss and one win, and the win is the trade he trusts less.
